See issue 217's\n// rewrite for the rationale.\n//\n// Run from any directory:  node --test tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs\n\nimport { test } from 'node:test';\nimport { strict as assert } from 'node:assert';\n\nconst DIR = process.env.SORAMECH_DIR || '/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech';\n\nconst VALID_SHAPES = new Set(['positional', 'none']);\n\n// {{{ check_spec(language, expected_ext)\nasync function check_spec(language, expected_ext) {\n  const mod = await import(`${DIR}/langs/${language}/spec.js`);\n  const spec = mod.LANGUAGE_SPEC;\n  assert.ok(spec, `LANGUAGE_SPEC export missing for ${language}`);\n  assert.equal(spec.name, language);\n  assert.equal(spec.file_ext, expected_ext);\n  assert.ok(VALID_SHAPES.has(spec.variadic_shape),\n    `unknown variadic_shape \"${spec.variadic_shape}\" for ${language}`);\n}\n// }}}\n\n// {{{ test('lua spec declares positional variadic')\ntest('lua spec declares positional variadic', async () => {\n  await check_spec('lua', '.lua');\n  const { LANGUAGE_SPEC } = await import(`${DIR}/langs/lua/spec.js`);\n  assert.equal(LANGUAGE_SPEC.variadic_shape, 'positional');\n});\n// }}}\n\n// {{{ test('bash spec declares positional variadic')\ntest('bash spec declares positional variadic', async () => {\n  await check_spec('bash', '.sh');\n  const { LANGUAGE_SPEC } = await import(`${DIR}/langs/bash/spec.js`);\n  assert.equal(LANGUAGE_SPEC.variadic_shape, 'positional');\n});\n// }}}\n\n// {{{ test('c spec declares positional variadic')\ntest('c spec declares positional variadic', async () => {\n  await check_spec('c', '.c');\n  const { LANGUAGE_SPEC } = await import(`${DIR}/langs/c/spec.js`);\n  assert.equal(LANGUAGE_SPEC.variadic_shape, 'positional');\n});\n// }}}\n",

    "originalFile":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline file_write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ compile_pipeline_check() — soramech-compile produces a portable artifact\n# Verifies issue 309's compile pipeline: bundles all spec.so + sources\n# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no\n# dependency on the project's cwd) and verifies it produces the same\n# output as the source map.\ncompile_pipeline_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local compiled=\"$map/compiled\"\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"compile pipeline (portable run)\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$compiled\"\n    if ! \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"who → World\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"input → 5\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"  %-44s SKIP — node not installed\\n\" \"parser tests (lua, bash)\"\n        return\n    fi\n    for tf in \"$DIR/tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs\"; do\n        local label\n        label=$(basename \"$tf\")\n        printf \"  %-44s \" \"$label\"\n        local out\n        out=$(SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\" 2>&1)\n        local rc=$?\n        if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL\\n\"\n            echo \"$out\" | sed 's/^/      /'\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"$label: node --test exit=$rc\")\n        fi\n    done\n}\nparser_tests\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",

{

        "input":{
          "content":"# 217 — Variadic ports and the language-spec variadic shape\n\n## Status\nopen — Part A and Part B mechanics are in the codebase; Part C is\nthe active design question\n\n## What this issue is now\n\nThe original issue was titled \"Concat box with per-input variadic\nports and auto-grow/shrink.\" That framing has aged out:\n\n- There is no dedicated **concat box kind**. `M.concat(sep, ...)`\n  lives in `libs/text.lua` and is invoked by any call box that\n  imports it. The variadic UI work was never specific to concat.\n- The original \"split returns a JSON-encoded array on the single\n  output wire\" story was a phase-2 transport assumption. Phase 3\n  (issue 312, same-language wire fast path) classifies each edge\n  and only JSON-encodes when crossing a language boundary. So\n  `M.split` returning a Lua array is correct in-language and the\n  runtime bridges if the downstream box is a different language.\n\nThe issue is now about the **editor's variadic-port mechanic** and\nhow it interacts with the **language spec** — specifically, what\nthe editor's `var` toggle means and what governs whether it's\noffered.\n\n## Part A — `libs/text.lua` *(shipped)*\n\n`libs/text.lua` ships `M.concat(sep, ...)`, `M.split(text, sep)`,\nand (via issue 237) `upper`, `lower`, `trim`, `replace`,\n`replace_first`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `length`,\n`substring`. All are pure string operations consumed by call\nboxes; no special box kind exists.\n\n`M.split` is most useful paired with the iterator box (issue 221)\nso each part fans out to its own dispatch. Without the iterator\nit's just \"an array on a wire\" — legitimate but flat.\n\n## Part B — Editor variadic data model *(shipped)*\n\nA box JSON can carry a `variadic_inputs` array of base names; slots\nare stored as `<base>_<index>` in the `inputs` array. The inspector\n(`assets/js/004-inspector.js`) implements:\n\n- `make_variadic(port_name)` — turn a plain port into a one-slot\n  variadic group (`text` → `text_0`).\n- `unmake_variadic(base)` — collapse back to a single port.\n- `add_variadic_slot(base)` — append `<base>_<last+1>` (auto-grow).\n- `remove_variadic_slot(slot_name)` — delete and renumber.\n- `auto_grow_after_set(box, slot_name)` — append a new empty slot\n  when the user uses the current last slot.\n\nAuto-grow triggers on wire-connect and on value-set. Shrinking is\nexplicit-only — `×` button per slot. Wire-disconnect and value-\nclear do **not** shrink, deliberately, so transient editing\ndoesn't lose structure.\n\nThe schema (`src/001-schema.lua`) accepts `variadic_inputs` as an\noptional array of strings.\n\n## Part C — What `var` actually means *(active design)*\n\n### Wrong model (rejected)\n\nThe earlier framing said: regex-parse each source file in the\neditor, mark functions whose signatures end in `...` / `\"$@\"` /\n`va_list` as \"variadic-capable,\" and gate the `var` toggle on\nthat per-function flag.\n\nThat model collapses on contact with the project's vision:\n\n1. **It's not a per-function fact.** Every Lua function accepts N\n   positional args. `function f(a)` called with five args silently\n   keeps the first; `...` in the signature is the *author's choice\n   to capture extras*, not a runtime constraint. Bash is the same\n   — every function gets `\"$@\"` whether it touches it or not. C\n   through the dispatch wrapper (issue 304) is the same —\n   `argc`/`argv` is the universal call shape.\n2. **It centralises language knowledge in the editor.** Per-\n   language regex parsers in the editor are exactly the\n   ossification the `langs/<name>/` model exists to prevent.\n   Adding a new language would mean writing a new regex.\n3. **It locks the editor to a static source view.** A function the\n   user is in the middle of editing might briefly not have `...`\n   in the signature; the editor would flicker the toggle on/off.\n\n### Right model: variadic shape is a language fact\n\nThe language declares its calling-convention shape once, in\n`langs/<name>/spec.js`:\n\n```js\nexport const LANGUAGE_SPEC = {\n  name: 'lua',\n  file_ext: '.lua',\n  variadic_shape: 'positional',\n};\n```\n\n`variadic_shape: 'positional'` means the language accepts N\npositional args at call time, period. Every shipped language today\n(Lua, Bash, C) declares this. Future languages with different\nshapes (Python `**kwargs`, streaming generators, tagged unions)\ndeclare their own shape — the editor's variadic UI eventually\ngrows variants for them, but `positional` covers everything we\nship.\n\nA language that genuinely cannot accept variadic input declares\n`variadic_shape: 'none'`, and the editor disables the `var` toggle\nfor all its boxes. We don't have one of those today.\n\n### Editor behaviour under this model\n\n- The `var` toggle on a port is gated by **language**, not by\n  function. For every Lua / Bash / C box today, the toggle is\n  available.\n- The user is responsible for matching wired arity to the\n  function's intent. The editor surfaces what the source declares\n  (via `parser.js`'s named parameters) so the user can see the\n  arity the author wrote. If they wire five inputs to a function\n  whose body only reads the first, that's a user choice — same\n  class as wiring a string into a port the function treats as a\n  number. The runtime doesn't police it.\n- Compile-time (issue 309) and validator (issue 002) checks\n  surface obvious mismatches as documentation, not as gates.\n\n### What `parser.js` does and doesn't do\n\n`langs/<name>/parser.js` continues to enumerate functions in a\nsource file and extract named parameter and return names. That\nfeeds the file browser. It does **not** compute any per-function\nvariadic property — the early `variadic_tail` field was removed\nin this issue's pass.\n\n### Implementation status\n\n- `langs/lua/spec.js`, `langs/bash/spec.js`, `langs/c/spec.js` —\n  shipped. Each exports `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with `variadic_shape:\n  'positional'`.\n- `langs/lua/parser.js`, `langs/bash/parser.js` — shipped without\n  `variadic_tail`. Still produce inputs/outputs for the file\n  browser.\n- `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` — shipped. Asserts every\n  spec.js exports a valid `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with a known\n  `variadic_shape`.\n- Inspector consumption of `LANGUAGE_SPEC.variadic_shape` —\n  **not yet wired**. Today the `var` toggle is offered\n  unconditionally; the gate-by-language step is the remaining\n  work.\n\n### Remaining work\n\n1. `assets/js/004-inspector.js::mk_port_display` — load the active\n   box's language spec (the same dynamic-import pattern used for\n   lexers), and hide the `var` button when\n   `variadic_shape !== 'positional'`. Today every shipped language\n   is positional, so this is a future-proofing step rather than a\n   visible change.\n2. Inspector renders the parsed signature near the box header so\n   the user always sees the function's declared arity. This is the\n   documentation half of the design — replaces the rejected \"gate\n   the toggle per function\" approach with \"show the arity, let the\n   user judge.\"\n3. Update `docs/005-language-specs.md` with a \"language spec for\n   the editor\" section pointing at `spec.js` as the canonical\n   home for editor-facing language facts (variadic shape, future\n   additions).\n\n## Future development ideas\n\n### Variadic shapes that aren't `positional`\n\n- `keyed` — Python `**kwargs`, Ruby keyword splats. Slot model is\n  `(key, value)` pairs, user labels per slot, not auto-numbered.\n- `tagged` — Rust enum lists, Haskell heterogeneous lists. Per-\n  slot `(tag, value)`.\n- `stream` — generators, channels, iterators. One slot, queued.\n  Closer to issue 213's queued-input model than to positional\n  variadic.\n\nEach shape has its own auto-grow rule and inspector controls. The\nlanguage spec declares which shape applies; the editor renders\naccordingly. None of these are shipped — the positional shape\ncovers every language so far. Captured here so the design door\nstays open.\n\n### Outputs\n\nThe single-output rule (issue 218) is unchanged.     "content":"# 217 — Variadic ports and the language-spec variadic shape\n\n## Status\nopen — Part A and Part B mechanics are in the codebase; Part C is\nthe active design question\n\n## What this issue is now\n\nThe original issue was titled \"Concat box with per-input variadic\nports and auto-grow/shrink.\" That framing has aged out:\n\n- There is no dedicated **concat box kind**. `M.concat(sep, ...)`\n  lives in `libs/text.lua` and is invoked by any call box that\n  imports it. The variadic UI work was never specific to concat.\n- The original \"split returns a JSON-encoded array on the single\n  output wire\" story was a phase-2 transport assumption. Phase 3\n  (issue 312, same-language wire fast path) classifies each edge\n  and only JSON-encodes when crossing a language boundary. So\n  `M.split` returning a Lua array is correct in-language and the\n  runtime bridges if the downstream box is a different language.\n\nThe issue is now about the **editor's variadic-port mechanic** and\nhow it interacts with the **language spec** — specifically, what\nthe editor's `var` toggle means and what governs whether it's\noffered.\n\n## Part A — `libs/text.lua` *(shipped)*\n\n`libs/text.lua` ships `M.concat(sep, ...)`, `M.split(text, sep)`,\nand (via issue 237) `upper`, `lower`, `trim`, `replace`,\n`replace_first`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `length`,\n`substring`. All are pure string operations consumed by call\nboxes; no special box kind exists.\n\n`M.split` is most useful paired with the iterator box (issue 221)\nso each part fans out to its own dispatch. Without the iterator\nit's just \"an array on a wire\" — legitimate but flat.\n\n## Part B — Editor variadic data model *(shipped)*\n\nA box JSON can carry a `variadic_inputs` array of base names; slots\nare stored as `<base>_<index>` in the `inputs` array. The inspector\n(`assets/js/004-inspector.js`) implements:\n\n- `make_variadic(port_name)` — turn a plain port into a one-slot\n  variadic group (`text` → `text_0`).\n- `unmake_variadic(base)` — collapse back to a single port.\n- `add_variadic_slot(base)` — append `<base>_<last+1>` (auto-grow).\n- `remove_variadic_slot(slot_name)` — delete and renumber.\n- `auto_grow_after_set(box, slot_name)` — append a new empty slot\n  when the user uses the current last slot.\n\nAuto-grow triggers on wire-connect and on value-set. Shrinking is\nexplicit-only — `×` button per slot. Wire-disconnect and value-\nclear do **not** shrink, deliberately, so transient editing\ndoesn't lose structure.\n\nThe schema (`src/001-schema.lua`) accepts `variadic_inputs` as an\noptional array of strings.\n\n## Part C — What `var` actually means *(active design)*\n\n### Wrong model (rejected)\n\nThe earlier framing said: regex-parse each source file in the\neditor, mark functions whose signatures end in `...` / `\"$@\"` /\n`va_list` as \"variadic-capable,\" and gate the `var` toggle on\nthat per-function flag.\n\nThat model collapses on contact with the project's vision:\n\n1. **It's not a per-function fact.** Every Lua function accepts N\n   positional args. `function f(a)` called with five args silently\n   keeps the first; `...` in the signature is the *author's choice\n   to capture extras*, not a runtime constraint. Bash is the same\n   — every function gets `\"$@\"` whether it touches it or not. C\n   through the dispatch wrapper (issue 304) is the same —\n   `argc`/`argv` is the universal call shape.\n2. **It centralises language knowledge in the editor.** Per-\n   language regex parsers in the editor are exactly the\n   ossification the `langs/<name>/` model exists to prevent.\n   Adding a new language would mean writing a new regex.\n3. **It locks the editor to a static source view.** A function the\n   user is in the middle of editing might briefly not have `...`\n   in the signature; the editor would flicker the toggle on/off.\n\n### Right model: variadic shape is a language fact\n\nThe language declares its calling-convention shape once, in\n`langs/<name>/spec.js`:\n\n```js\nexport const LANGUAGE_SPEC = {\n  name: 'lua',\n  file_ext: '.lua',\n  variadic_shape: 'positional',\n};\n```\n\n`variadic_shape: 'positional'` means the language accepts N\npositional args at call time, period. Every shipped language today\n(Lua, Bash, C) declares this. Future languages with different\nshapes (Python `**kwargs`, streaming generators, tagged unions)\ndeclare their own shape — the editor's variadic UI eventually\ngrows variants for them, but `positional` covers everything we\nship.\n\nA language that genuinely cannot accept variadic input declares\n`variadic_shape: 'none'`, and the editor disables the `var` toggle\nfor all its boxes. We don't have one of those today.\n\n### Editor behaviour under this model\n\n- The `var` toggle on a port is gated by **language**, not by\n  function. For every Lua / Bash / C box today, the toggle is\n  available.\n- The user is responsible for matching wired arity to the\n  function's intent. The editor surfaces what the source declares\n  (via `parser.js`'s named parameters) so the user can see the\n  arity the author wrote. If they wire five inputs to a function\n  whose body only reads the first, that's a user choice — same\n  class as wiring a string into a port the function treats as a\n  number. The runtime doesn't police it.\n- Compile-time (issue 309) and validator (issue 002) checks\n  surface obvious mismatches as documentation, not as gates.\n\n### What `parser.js` does and doesn't do\n\n`langs/<name>/parser.js` continues to enumerate functions in a\nsource file and extract named parameter and return names. That\nfeeds the file browser. It does **not** compute any per-function\nvariadic property — the early `variadic_tail` field was removed\nin this issue's pass.\n\n### Implementation status\n\n- `langs/lua/spec.js`, `langs/bash/spec.js`, `langs/c/spec.js` —\n  shipped. Each exports `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with `variadic_shape:\n  'positional'`.\n- `langs/lua/parser.js`, `langs/bash/parser.js` — shipped without\n  `variadic_tail`. Still produce inputs/outputs for the file\n  browser.\n- `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` — shipped. Asserts every\n  spec.js exports a valid `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with a known\n  `variadic_shape`.\n- Inspector consumption of `LANGUAGE_SPEC.variadic_shape` —\n  **not yet wired**. Today the `var` toggle is offered\n  unconditionally; the gate-by-language step is the remaining\n  work.\n\n### Remaining work\n\n1. `assets/js/004-inspector.js::mk_port_display` — load the active\n   box's language spec (the same dynamic-import pattern used for\n   lexers), and hide the `var` button when\n   `variadic_shape !== 'positional'`. Today every shipped language\n   is positional, so this is a future-proofing step rather than a\n   visible change.\n2. Inspector renders the parsed signature near the box header so\n   the user always sees the function's declared arity. This is the\n   documentation half of the design — replaces the rejected \"gate\n   the toggle per function\" approach with \"show the arity, let the\n   user judge.\"\n3. Update `docs/005-language-specs.md` with a \"language spec for\n   the editor\" section pointing at `spec.js` as the canonical\n   home for editor-facing language facts (variadic shape, future\n   additions).\n\n## Future development ideas\n\n### Variadic shapes that aren't `positional`\n\n- `keyed` — Python `**kwargs`, Ruby keyword splats. Slot model is\n  `(key, value)` pairs, user labels per slot, not auto-numbered.\n- `tagged` — Rust enum lists, Haskell heterogeneous lists. Per-\n  slot `(tag, value)`.\n- `stream` — generators, channels, iterators. One slot, queued.\n  Closer to issue 213's queued-input model than to positional\n  variadic.\n\nEach shape has its own auto-grow rule and inspector controls. The\nlanguage spec declares which shape applies; the editor renders\naccordingly. None of these are shipped — the positional shape\ncovers every language so far. Captured here so the design door\nstays open.\n\n### Outputs\n\nThe single-output rule (issue 218) is unchanged. Variadic is an\ninput-side concern.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `libs/text.lua` — Part A library functions\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — Part B variadic mechanics, future\n  home for the spec-driven `var` gate\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — accepts `variadic_inputs`\n- `langs/lua/spec.js`, `langs/bash/spec.js`, `langs/c/spec.js` —\n  the language-level `variadic_shape` declarations\n- `langs/lua/parser.js`, `langs/bash/parser.js` — function\n  enumeration (no per-function variadic detection)\n- `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` — spec.js contract tests\n- `issues/231-move-signature-parsers-into-langs.md` — moved\n  signature parsing into `langs/<name>/parser.js`\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — supersedes the\n  old \"JSON-encode every wire\" story Part A was framed against\n- `issues/221-iterator-box.md` — the canonical companion to\n  `M.split` for fan-out\n",

          "old_string":"### 2026-05-19 — parser tests + Node runner integration\n\n`tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs` (10 cases) and\n`tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs` (9 cases) added under Node's\nbuilt-in `node:test`. They run via `scripts/run-tests.sh`, which\ngained a `parser_tests()` section that calls\n`SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\"` for each file and folds\nthe result into the existing pass/fail summary.\n\n`SORAMECH_DIR=...` overrides the project root when running outside\nthe default install path. Argv would collide with `node --test`'s\nfile-list parsing, so an env var is the right channel.\n\nVerified failure detection by temporarily inverting the Lua\nparser's variadic-tail check — the lua test failed as expected and\nthe failure surfaced through the shell runner.",
          "new_string":"### 2026-05-19 — parser tests + Node runner integration\n\n`tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs` and `tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs`\nadded under Node's built-in `node:test`. They run via\n`scripts/run-tests.sh`, which gained a `parser_tests()` section\nthat calls `SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\"` for each file\nand folds the result into the existing pass/fail summary.\n\n`SORAMECH_DIR=...` overrides the project root when running outside\nthe default install path. Argv would collide with `node --test`'s\nfile-list parsing, so an env var is the right channel.\n\nVerified failure detection by temporarily inverting a parser\ncheck — the relevant test failed as expected and the failure\nsurfaced through the shell runner.\n\n### 2026-05-19 — language-spec test, variadic_tail retired\n\nThe earlier pass added a `variadic_tail` field to both parsers\nalong with assertions in the parser tests. That model — per-\nfunction detection of variadic capability by source regex — was\nfundamentally wrong for the project's vision (every shipped\nlanguage already accepts N positional args at call time; \"is this\nfunction variadic\" is a question the runtime doesn't care about).\nSee issue 217's rewrite for the full reasoning.\n\nThe fix in this pass:\n\n- `variadic_tail` removed from `langs/lua/parser.js` and\n  `langs/bash/parser.js`. The parsers still extract named\n  parameters and outputs; the `...` token is still stripped from\n  inputs so the editor shows only named ports.\n- `tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs` and\n  `tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs` had their variadic_tail\n  assertions removed; they now lock the trimmed contract.\n- `langs/lua/spec.js`, `langs/bash/spec.js`, `langs/c/spec.js` —\n  new. Each exports `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with `variadic_shape:\n  'positional'`. This is the canonical home for editor-facing\n  language metadata.\n- `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` — new. Asserts every\n  spec.js exports a valid `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with a known\n  `variadic_shape`.\n\n10 / 10 passing in the full runner.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/232-test-coverage-map.md"

{

        "type":"tool_result",
        "content":"1\t# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\n8\thave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\n9\taccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n10\t\n11\t## Concept\n12\t\n13\t### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks\n14\t\n15\tEach box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph\n16\tloads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing\n17\tdeclaration: \"the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value\n18\tinto this consumer's named input slot.\" The producer never owns a\n19\tslot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.\n20\t\n21\tWhen a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into\n22\tevery downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N\n23\tpushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into\n24\tthe same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same\n25\tpush-into-input-slot mechanic.\n26\t\n27\tSlots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker\n28\tthread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs\n29\t(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot\n30\taddresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not\n31\tshared memory.\n32\t\n33\t### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable\n34\t\n35\tA **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's\n36\tinput slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every\n37\tdownstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're\n38\tjust stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the\n39\tdispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot\n40\tholds at least one value).\n41\t\n42\tThe **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any\n43\tcounter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so\n44\ton. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and\n45\tgo.\n46\t\n47\tThis is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N\n48\ttimes where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply\n49\t(possibly 1, possibly thousands). The difference is just what the\n50\ttask does:\n51\t- **Plain call task**: invoke spec on the popped values, push the\n52\t  return to outputs.\n53\t- **Iterator task**: read box's counter, route the popped value to\n54\t  output port `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.\n55\t  No spec invocation.\n56\t- **Comparator task**: invoke spec on the popped values, compare\n57\t  the return against `comparand`, route to the matching `lt` /\n58\t  `eq` / `gt` branch.\n59\t\n60\t### All slots are ring buffers; read mode varies\n61\t\n62\tThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\n63\teach of `cell_capacity` bytes. The number of cells (`n_cells`) and\n64\tthe read mode are both compile-time properties of the input port:\n65\t\n66\t- **1-cell + peek mode**: the value the producer wrote stays in the\n67\t  cell. Tasks read via `slot_peek` — read without draining — and\n68\t  every subsequent task on this consumer reads the same value\n69\t  unless the producer overwrites it. Used for **single-push wires**\n70\t  (a literal, or a wire from a producer box whose invocation count\n71\t  is exactly 1). Multiple consumer tasks read the value as many\n72\t  times as needed; the cell is never empty.\n73\t- **N-cell + pop mode**: a queue. Producers push; consumers\n74\t  `slot_pop` — drain one cell per task. Used for **multi-push wires**:\n75\t  any wire whose producer has more than one task invocation\n76\t  during the run. The producer's pushes accumulate, the consumer\n77\t  drains in pop order.\n78\t\n79\tCompile-time analysis classifies each wire. A producer is\n80\t\"runs-once\" if no transitive ancestor is an iterator; otherwise\n81\tit's \"runs-N-times.\" Wires from runs-once producers get 1-cell\n82\tpeek slots; wires from runs-N-times producers get N-cell pop slots.\n83\t\n84\t`n_cells` for pop slots is sized for worst-case backlog (or a\n85\tdefault like 64 with growth on demand). Lists grow if the producer\n86\toutruns the consumer past the pre-allocation.\n87\t\n88\tFan-in: multiple producers pushing into the same N-cell pop slot\n89\tland in arrival order. The consumer pops FIFO unless the cell\n90\tcarries an ordering tag (see \"Cell tagging\" below).\n91\t\n92\t### Atomic-counter slot mode\n93\t\n94\tA slot allocated with `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` carries a single\n95\t4-byte unsigned integer cell, read via a special op:\n96\t\n97\t```c\n98\tuint32_t slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);\n99\t// Returns the current value mod `mod`, then atomically increments\n100\t// the underlying counter. Concurrent readers each get a distinct\n101\t// value. Counter wraps at 2^32; mod handles N-branch routing.\n102\t```\n103\t\n104\tUsed for iterator counters (issue 304): the iterator box has an\n105\tauto-allocated `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot at load time; the\n106\tdispatch action calls `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_branches)`\n107\tto pick its output branch. Multiple iterator tasks can read\n108\tconcurrently from the same counter slot in parallel — each gets a\n109\tunique routing index — without any per-box mutable state and\n110\twithout the serial dependency of a self-push counter.\n111\t\n112\tThe slot's \"cell\" is just an `atomic_uint32_t`. No push is ever\n113\tperformed; reads do the work. From the dispatch action's\n114\tperspective it's just another slot; from the slot store's\n115\tperspective the read op is special-cased.\n116\t\n117\t### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)\n118\t\n119\tA cell can optionally carry a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\n120\tsize and data:\n121\t\n122\t```\n123\tCell layout (N-cell pop slot)\n124\tOffset  Size  Field\n125\t------  ----  -----\n126\t0       4     filled_size\n127\t4       4     tag      (0 if untagged; iterator counter snapshot otherwise)\n128\t8       …     data\n129\t```\n130\t\n131\tSlots created for wires from parallel iterators (issue 304) are\n132\ttagged. Pop on a tagged slot returns the cell with the lowest tag,\n133\tnot the head cell — preserving iterator-counter order across pushes\n134\tthat arrived out of order from parallel iterator workers.\n135\t\n136\tUntagged slots default tag to 0 and pop FIFO at no extra cost. The\n137\ttag-aware pop is a per-slot mode flag set at allocation time.\n138\t\n139\t### Asynchrony\n140\tThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\n141\tfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\n142\tis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n143\t\n144\t## Slot layout\n145\t\n146\tEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\n147\tbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n148\t\n149\t```\n150\tSlot header\n151\tOffset  Size  Field\n152\t------  ----  -----\n153\t0       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n154\t4       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation)\n155\t8       4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n156\t12      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n157\t16      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n158\t17      3     _pad\n159\t20      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n160\t```\n161\t\n162\tEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\n163\tbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\n164\tslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\n165\tsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\n166\thow big it needs the cells.\n167\t\n168\t`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n169\t(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\n170\tspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\n171\tif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\n172\tchanging the API.\n173\t\n174\tWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\n175\tadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\n176\tsee the complete value at the head cell.\n177\t\n178\t## Lifetime\n179\t\n180\tSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\n181\tfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\n182\tcounting and no end-of-stream propagation — the slot is freed\n183\twhen the run ends, alongside its owning box.\n184\t\n185\tRun termination is governed entirely by the pool's active-task\n186\tcounter (issue 301): when no task is running and no further spawns\n187\tare pending, the run is over. There's nothing the slot store needs\n188\tto track to make this work.\n189\t\n190\t### No wait lists\n191\t\n192\tTasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch\n193\tlayer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they\n194\tnever block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the\n195\tspawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,\n196\tno per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.\n197\t\n198\t## Backing store\n199\t\n200\tSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\n201\tper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\n202\thands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\n203\tsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\n204\tit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n205\t\n206\tSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\n207\theader mutations. There is no allocator-wide mutex on the\n208\tread/write path; only the per-size-class free lists in the\n209\tallocator have their own locks.\n210\t\n211\t## Slot creation\n212\t\n213\tSlot creation happens at **graph load**, not per task. The graph\n214\tloader walks every box, allocates one ring buffer per input port,\n215\tand parks the slot on the box's per-port slot table. The dispatch\n216\tlayer never allocates new slots at runtime in the steady state —\n217\tall slots that will ever exist are created up front.\n218\t\n219\t```c\n220\tslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n221\t```\n222\t\n223\t`cell_capacity` and `n_cells` come from compile-time analysis of\n224\tthe graph. Boxes downstream of iterators get larger `n_cells` to\n225\tabsorb the iterator's worst-case backlog.\n226\t\n227\tIf a slot's pre-allocated `n_cells` proves too small at runtime\n228\t(producer outpaces consumer beyond the pre-allocation), the slot's\n229\tring grows — see \"Allocation strategy\" below.\n230\t\n231\t## C API surface\n232\t\n233\t```c\n234\tslot_id_t slot_alloc       (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells, int flags);\n235\tvoid      slot_push        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size, uint32_t tag);\n236\tint       slot_peek        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // 1-cell: read without draining\n237\tint       slot_pop         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // N-cell: drain head (or lowest-tag)\n238\tuint32_t  slot_read_inc    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);            // SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER only\n239\tint       slot_has_value   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);                          // for spawn-rule check\n240\t```\n241\t\n242\tFlags include:\n243\t- `SLOT_TAGGED`: cells carry ordering tags; `slot_pop` returns the\n244\t  lowest-tag cell.\n245\t- `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`: slot holds a single atomic uint32; reads\n246\t  via `slot_read_inc` only. `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop`\n247\t  are not valid on atomic-counter slots.\n248\t\n249\tPush always takes a `tag` argument; untagged slots ignore it (or\n250\ttreat 0 as \"no order\").\n251\t\n252\t1-cell peek slot use: producer `push` once at startup (literal) or\n253\twhen its single invocation completes (single-push wire). All\n254\tconsumer tasks `peek` to read the value as many times as their box\n255\truns. The cell is never empty after the initial push.\n256\t\n257\tN-cell pop slot use: producers `push` repeatedly. Consumer tasks\n258\t`pop` one cell each. For tagged slots, `pop` returns the\n259\tlowest-tag cell; for untagged, FIFO. Pop on an empty slot is a\n260\tbug — the spawn rule guarantees the slot is non-empty before a\n261\ttask spawns.\n262\t\n263\tThere is no `slot_ref` / `slot_unref` — slot lifetime is the run.\n264\t\n265\t## Submission timing\n266\t\n267\tTasks are spawned dynamically in response to slot pushes. Each box\n268\thas small per-box state used by the dispatch layer:\n269\t\n270\t```\n271\tbox_runtime_state {\n272\t    slot_id_t  *input_slots;     // one per input port (set at load)\n273\t    int        *port_modes;      // PEEK or POP, per input port\n274\t    int         n_inputs;\n275\t    slot_id_t   counter_slot;    // iterator only: SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER slot;\n276\t                                 // 0 / unused otherwise\n277\t};\n278\t```\n279\t\n280\tThe spawning rule:\n281\t- When a producer pushes to one of a box's input slots, the\n282\t  dispatch layer checks **does every input slot have a value\n283\t  available?** \"Available\" means:\n284\t  - For peek-mode (1-cell) slots: cell has been written at least\n285\t    once. Once a peek slot is filled, it stays available — every\n286\t    subsequent spawn-check on this box passes the peek-port check.\n287\t  - For pop-mode (N-cell) slots: queue is non-empty.\n288\t- If yes, spawn a `dispatch_task_t` and submit to the pool. The\n289\t  task pops (or peeks) one value from each input slot when it\n290\t  runs.\n291\t- Each push that completes the input set triggers exactly one\n292\t  spawn. Multiple pushes accumulate in pop slots; each pop\n293\t  consumes one, and if more remain, the next push (or check)\n294\t  re-fires the spawn rule.\n295\t\n296\tThis makes the pool's queue the rate buffer: pushes accumulate\n297\tin pop slots (possibly multiple per slot), and one task per\n298\taccumulated value gets spawned.\n299\t\n300\tTasks never block on slots. They're spawned after inputs are\n301\tready, run to completion, and disappear. Blocking-and-waking\n302\tmachinery is unnecessary — the spawn-on-arrival rule is the\n303\tsynchronization primitive.\n304\t\n305\tThe pool's queue is the only queue. There is no separate \"blocked\n306\ttasks\" structure.\n307\t\n308\t## Allocation strategy: size-class free lists with coalescing fallback\n309\t\n310\tThe slot store uses a segregated free-list allocator. The map is\n311\tanalyzed at compile time to enumerate every distinct slot size the\n312\tgraph will need (each call box declares its output slot size; each\n313\tqueued-input ring declares its total size from cell capacity × queue\n314\tdepth). The allocator builds one free list per distinct size class.\n315\t\n316\tVariable-size and unknown-size payloads (a long LLM response, an\n317\tarray whose length is not known until runtime) are handled by a\n318\tseparate **large-value heap** described below — not by allocating\n319\thuge slots up front.\n320\t\n321\t### The lists\n322\tEach size class is an array (or linked list) of free slots of exactly\n323\tthat size. At startup, each list is pre-populated with enough slots\n324\tto cover the static box count for that size. Lists grow during the\n325\trun if demand exceeds the pre-allocation.\n326\t\n327\tEach list has its own mutex — allocation and deallocation in different\n328\tsize classes never contend with each other.\n329\t\n330\t### Allocation\n331\tGiven a request for size N bytes:\n332\t1. Find the smallest size class with `class_size ≥ N`.\n333\t2. If that class has a free slot, pop it. Done.\n334\t3. Otherwise, try the next larger size class. Repeat.\n335\t4. If a larger class hits, the slot is oversized for the request.\n336\t   Try to slice the unused tail into a residual slot. If the residual\n337\t   is at least as large as the smallest size class, push it onto that\n338\t   class's list. Otherwise skip the slice — oversize the allocation\n339\t   and live with the waste until the slot is freed.\n340\t5. If no size class has a free slot, attempt to coalesce: walk the\n341\t   address-ordered chunk list looking for adjacent free chunks that\n342\t   together meet the requested size. If found, merge them and return\n343\t   the combined chunk.\n344\t6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and\n345\t   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.\n346\t7. After steps 5 or 6 complete, queue a deferred cleanup task on the\n347\t   pool. Cleanup runs on a worker thread later and walks the\n348\t   chunk list to opportunistically coalesce contiguous free chunks\n349\t   into the largest possible chunks. Cleanup is best-effort — it\n350\t   does not block any other thread. If memory fragments faster than\n351\t   cleanup can keep up, the next allocation grows the heap; that's\n352\t   fine.\n353\t\n354\t### Deallocation\n355\tWhen refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's\n356\tfree list. The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:\n357\tcheck the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge\n358\tthem and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.\n359\tThis is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps\n360\tsmall-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred\n361\tcleanup task to run.\n362\t\n363\t### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)\n364\tCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in\n365\tmemory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.\n366\t\n367\tTwo viable representations:\n368\t\n369\t- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in\n370\t  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.\n371\t  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.\n372\t- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start\n373\t  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and\n374\t  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to\n375\t  scan.\n376\t\n377\tThe linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for\n378\tsplits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows\n379\tlist traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary\n380\tindex — the API doesn't change.\n381\t\n382\t### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)\n383\t\n384\tFor values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM\n385\tresponses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound\n386\tis not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value\n387\tdirectly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:\n388\t\n389\t```\n390\t{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }\n391\t```\n392\t\n393\t`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a\n394\tplain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.\n395\tWhen a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:\n396\t1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.\n397\t2. Writes the bytes there.\n398\t3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.\n399\t\n400\tThe consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,\n401\tcopies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's\n402\trefcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the\n403\tlarge-value-heap region.\n404\t\n405\tThe slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.\n406\tThe two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still\n407\tsupporting unbounded outputs.\n408\t\n409\tA box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as\n410\t\"variable-size\" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the\n411\tfixed-size path with no indirection.\n412\t\n413\t### Growth\n414\tWhen all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy\n415\ta request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,\n416\tdividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class\n417\tlists. Plain heap memory is fine — no spec needs cross-process access\n418\tto slot memory.\n419\t\n420\t### Why this design\n421\t- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single\n422\t  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.\n423\t- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the\n424\t  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply\n425\t  not split.\n426\t- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,\n427\t  and it costs nothing on the common path.\n428\t- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never\n429\t  fires.\n430\t\n431\t## No type tags\n432\t\n433\tSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\n434\treads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\n435\ton each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\n436\tcompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\n437\tbuild time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not\n438\tneed to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything\n439\telse. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.\n440\t\n441\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n442\t1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n443\t2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n444\t   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n445\t3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n446\t   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n447\t4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n448\t   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n449\t\n450\t## Relevant files\n451\t- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n452\t- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n453\t- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n454\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n455\t- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n456\t  ring-buffer slots implement\n457\t- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n458\t\n459\t## Implementation log\n460\t\n461\t### Core milestone — 2026-05-12\n462\t\n463\tWhat shipped:\n464\t- `src/009-slot-store.h` — the public API exactly as the design\n465\t  describes: `slot_alloc` / `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop` /\n466\t  `slot_read_inc` / `slot_has_value` / `slot_fill_count`. Plus the\n467\t  store lifecycle pair and a small inspection helper for tests.\n468\t- `src/009-slot-store.c` — implementation. Plain-malloc per slot\n469\t  (size-class free lists deferred); ring slots and atomic-counter\n470\t  slots both supported; the SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED variant of pop scans\n471\t  for the lowest-tag filled cell. Per-slot spinlock via\n472\t  `atomic_flag`. Atomic counter via `atomic_fetch_add_explicit`,\n473\t  no lock.\n474\t- `tests/009-slot-store-test.c` — 12 unit tests covering peek\n475\t  semantics, FIFO pop, tagged pop ordering (in-order and\n476\t  interleaved), atomic counter (sequential + 8-thread concurrent),\n477\t  bad-argument paths, ring-full / empty edge cases, and a\n478\t  multi-thread producer/consumer race over 5000 values.\n479\t- Makefile additions: `test` target builds test binaries via a\n480\t  pattern rule and runs them. Per-test prerequisites listed\n481\t  explicitly so each binary links the minimal set of source `.o`s.\n482\t- File index counter advanced to `009`.\n483\t\n484\tVerified clean build and 12/12 tests pass in `make STRICT=1`\n485\t(`-Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic`).\n486\t\n487\tWhat's deferred to a follow-on within 302:\n488\t- **Size-class free lists with coalescing.** The current\n489\t  implementation `malloc`s each slot independently. That's correct\n490\t  but unoptimized. Slots are allocated once at graph load and never\n491\t  freed until run end, so under the current usage pattern free-list\n492\t  reuse buys nothing. Lands once profiling justifies it (or once\n493\t  long-running maps surface allocation pressure).\n494\t- **Large-value heap for variable-size payloads.** Slots currently\n495\t  store fixed-size cells; very large outputs (multi-MB LLM\n496\t  responses, dynamically-sized arrays) will need the two-tier\n497\t  scheme described under \"Large-value heap\" above. Blocks no\n498\t  in-flight phase 3 work until a graph wants variable-size outputs.\n499\t\n500\tNeither deferred item blocks 301 / 304 / 305 / 306 / 307 / 308.\n501\t\n502\t### Large-value heap milestone — 2026-05-19\n503\t\n504\tThe variable-size payload follow-on landed in two layers:\n505\t\n506\t1. **`src/015-large-value-heap.{c,h}`** — chunked arena allocator.\n507\t   Default 64 KB chunks; oversized allocations (larger than the\n508\t   default chunk) get their own exact-fit chunk so one large value\n509\t   doesn't bloat the regular bump chunks. Pointer stability is the\n510\t   load-bearing property: chunks never move once allocated, so a\n511\t   consumer's pointer survives any number of subsequent producer\n512\t   allocations. Eight unit tests in\n513\t   `tests/015-large-value-heap-test.c` cover the create/destroy\n514\t   round-trip, single + multi alloc within a chunk, oversized\n515\t   allocations getting their own chunks, pointer stability across\n516\t   forced growth, zero-size allocations returning non-NULL, the\n517\t   stats accessors, and an eight-thread / eight-thousand-alloc\n518\t   concurrency stress test that asserts every returned pointer is\n519\t   unique and writable.\n520\t\n521\t2. **Slot-store integration.** Added `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` to\n522\t   `slot_alloc`. Cell layout for LARGE_VALUE slots is\n523\t   `filled_size (4 bytes) + pad/tag (4 bytes) + stable pointer\n524\t   (8 bytes)` — the 8-byte payload offset keeps the pointer\n525\t   naturally aligned regardless of whether SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED is\n526\t   also set. The slot store lazy-creates one shared lvh heap on\n527\t   the first LARGE_VALUE allocation; the heap is destroyed\n528\t   alongside the store. Push allocates from the heap *outside*\n529\t   the slot spinlock (the heap has its own mutex; nesting is\n530\t   fine, but reducing time-under-spinlock keeps the lock fast for\n531\t   other producers). Peek and pop follow the cell's pointer and\n532\t   memcpy the requested bytes back into the caller's buffer.\n533\t\n534\tFour new slot-store tests cover the new path:\n535\t`large_value_push_pop` (100 KB payload, double-peek, then pop);\n536\t`large_value_buf_too_small` (oversized payload + small dest →\n537\t-1, cell preserved); `large_value_multi_push_fifo` (three\n538\tdifferent-size values pushed and popped in order); and\n539\t`large_value_tagged_ordering` (LARGE_VALUE + TAGGED → pops\n540\treturn lowest-tag-first with bytes intact).\n541\t\n542\tWhat this unblocks: any box that wants to emit a variable-size\n543\toutput can now declare its downstream consumer slots with\n544\tSLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE and produce payloads whose size isn't\n545\tknown at graph-load time. The wiring from declared box output\n546\ttype to the LARGE_VALUE flag in `graph_attach_runtime` lands as\n547\ta follow-on once a fixture or real graph requires it; the\n548\tfoundation is in place.\n549\t\n550\t### Producer-driven LARGE_VALUE wiring — 2026-05-19\n551\t\n552\tThe \"wiring from declared box output type\" deferred above is\n553\tnow in place. During `graph_attach_runtime`, each consumer\n554\tinput slot's flags get OR'd with `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` if any\n555\tproducer feeding that port declares `output_capacity == 0`. The\n556\trule covers both data boxes (which default to 0 because the\n557\tfield isn't in their JSON schema) and call boxes that opt into\n558\tvariable-size output by setting `\"output_capacity\": 0`. A\n559\tmixed-language fan-in where any producer is variable-size\n560\tupgrades the whole slot to LARGE_VALUE — the conservative call,\n561\tsince the slot can only carry one format and the LVH path\n562\thandles small payloads correctly too.\n563\t\n564\tA new test in `tests/010-graph-loader-test.c`\n565\t(`variable_size_producer_lvh_wiring`) attaches the hello fixture\n566\twith a deliberately tight default_cell_bytes of 512, then\n567\tasserts a 2 KB push succeeds on greet's `name` port (fed by\n568\tdata box `who`) and fails on greet's `salutation` port (literal\n569\tonly, no producer). The discriminator is the slot's capacity:\n570\twithout LARGE_VALUE the 2 KB push exceeds 512 and is rejected;\n571\twith it the heap absorbs the bytes and the push lands.\n572\t\n573\tThe remaining phase-3 checklist item \"Variable-size outputs\n574\twork via the large-value heap\" is now satisfied end-to-end at\n575\tthe slot-store boundary. A graph fixture that exercises the\n576\tpath on the dispatch side — a Lua box returning a multi-KB\n577\tstring and a downstream box reading it — is a one-line fixture\n578\taddition and lands with the 6-more-integration-fixtures task.\n579\t\n580\tWhat's still deferred within 302:\n581\t- **Size-class free lists with coalescing.** Still no need.\n582\t- **Per-allocation free in the large-value heap.** The heap\n583\t  grows monotonically for the life of a run. Long-running\n584\t  iterator loops that emit large values will pin memory until\n585\t  run end. Acceptable for current fixtures; a size-class\n586\t  allocator with eager-coalesce is the upgrade path if profiling\n587\t  flags it.\n588\t",
