      "content":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks\n\nEach box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph\nloads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing\ndeclaration: \"the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value\ninto this consumer's named input slot.\" The producer never owns a\nslot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.\n\nWhen a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into\nevery downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N\npushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into\nthe same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same\npush-into-input-slot mechanic.\n\nSlots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker\nthread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs\n(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot\naddresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not\nshared memory.\n\n### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable\n\nA **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's\ninput slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every\ndownstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're\njust stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the\ndispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot\nholds at least one value).\n\nThe **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any\ncounter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so\non. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and\ngo.\n\nThis is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N\ntimes where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply\n(possibly 1, possibly thousands). The difference is just what the\ntask does:\n- **Plain call task**: invoke spec on the popped values, push the\n  return to outputs.\n- **Iterator task**: read box's counter, route the popped value to\n  output port `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.\n  No spec invocation.\n- **Comparator task**: invoke spec on the popped values, compare\n  the return against `comparand`, route to the matching `lt` /\n  `eq` / `gt` branch.\n\n### All slots are ring buffers; read mode varies\n\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\neach of `cell_capacity` bytes. The number of cells (`n_cells`) and\nthe read mode are both compile-time properties of the input port:\n\n- **1-cell + peek mode**: the value the producer wrote stays in the\n  cell. Tasks read via `slot_peek` — read without draining — and\n  every subsequent task on this consumer reads the same value\n  unless the producer overwrites it. Used for **single-push wires**\n  (a literal, or a wire from a producer box whose invocation count\n  is exactly 1). Multiple consumer tasks read the value as many\n  times as needed; the cell is never empty.\n- **N-cell + pop mode**: a queue. Producers push; consumers\n  `slot_pop` — drain one cell per task. Used for **multi-push wires**:\n  any wire whose producer has more than one task invocation\n  during the run. The producer's pushes accumulate, the consumer\n  drains in pop order.\n\nCompile-time analysis classifies each wire. A producer is\n\"runs-once\" if no transitive ancestor is an iterator; otherwise\nit's \"runs-N-times.\" Wires from runs-once producers get 1-cell\npeek slots; wires from runs-N-times producers get N-cell pop slots.\n\n`n_cells` for pop slots is sized for worst-case backlog (or a\ndefault like 64 with growth on demand). Lists grow if the producer\noutruns the consumer past the pre-allocation.\n\nFan-in: multiple producers pushing into the same N-cell pop slot\nland in arrival order. The consumer pops FIFO unless the cell\ncarries an ordering tag (see \"Cell tagging\" below).\n\n### Atomic-counter slot mode\n\nA slot allocated with `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` carries a single\n4-byte unsigned integer cell, read via a special op:\n\n```c\nuint32_t slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);\n// Returns the current value mod `mod`, then atomically increments\n// the underlying counter. Concurrent readers each get a distinct\n// value. Counter wraps at 2^32; mod handles N-branch routing.\n```\n\nUsed for iterator counters (issue 304): the iterator box has an\nauto-allocated `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot at load time; the\ndispatch action calls `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_branches)`\nto pick its output branch. Multiple iterator tasks can read\nconcurrently from the same counter slot in parallel — each gets a\nunique routing index — without any per-box mutable state and\nwithout the serial dependency of a self-push counter.\n\nThe slot's \"cell\" is just an `atomic_uint32_t`. No push is ever\nperformed; reads do the work. From the dispatch action's\nperspective it's just another slot; from the slot store's\nperspective the read op is special-cased.\n\n### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)\n\nA cell can optionally carry a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\nsize and data:\n\n```\nCell layout (N-cell pop slot)\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     filled_size\n4       4     tag      (0 if untagged; iterator counter snapshot otherwise)\n8       …     data\n```\n\nSlots created for wires from parallel iterators (issue 304) are\ntagged. Pop on a tagged slot returns the cell with the lowest tag,\nnot the head cell — preserving iterator-counter order across pushes\nthat arrived out of order from parallel iterator workers.\n\nUntagged slots default tag to 0 and pop FIFO at no extra cost. The\ntag-aware pop is a per-slot mode flag set at allocation time.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\nbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n\n```\nSlot header\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n4       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation)\n8       4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n12      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n16      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n17      3     _pad\n20      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n```\n\nEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\nbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\nslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\nsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\nhow big it needs the cells.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\nspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\nif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\nWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\nadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\nsee the complete value at the head cell.\n\n## Lifetime\n\nSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\nfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\ncounting and no end-of-stream propagation — the slot is freed\nwhen the run ends, alongside its owning box.\n\nRun termination is governed entirely by the pool's active-task\ncounter (issue 301): when no task is running and no further spawns\nare pending, the run is over. There's nothing the slot store needs\nto track to make this work.\n\n### No wait lists\n\nTasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch\nlayer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they\nnever block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the\nspawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,\nno per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\nper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\nhands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\nsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\nit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n\nSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\nheader mutations. There is no allocator-wide mutex on the\nread/write path; only the per-size-class free lists in the\nallocator have their own locks.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens at **graph load**, not per task. The graph\nloader walks every box, allocates one ring buffer per input port,\nand parks the slot on the box's per-port slot table. The dispatch\nlayer never allocates new slots at runtime in the steady state —\nall slots that will ever exist are created up front.\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n```\n\n`cell_capacity` and `n_cells` come from compile-time analysis of\nthe graph. Boxes downstream of iterators get larger `n_cells` to\nabsorb the iterator's worst-case backlog.\n\nIf a slot's pre-allocated `n_cells` proves too small at runtime\n(producer outpaces consumer beyond the pre-allocation), the slot's\nring grows — see \"Allocation strategy\" below.\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc       (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells, int flags);\nvoid      slot_push        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size, uint32_t tag);\nint       slot_peek        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // 1-cell: read without draining\nint       slot_pop         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // N-cell: drain head (or lowest-tag)\nuint32_t  slot_read_inc    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);            // SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER only\nint       slot_has_value   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);                          // for spawn-rule check\n```\n\nFlags include:\n- `SLOT_TAGGED`: cells carry ordering tags; `slot_pop` returns the\n  lowest-tag cell.\n- `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`: slot holds a single atomic uint32; reads\n  via `slot_read_inc` only. `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop`\n  are not valid on atomic-counter slots.\n\nPush always takes a `tag` argument; untagged slots ignore it (or\ntreat 0 as \"no order\").\n\n1-cell peek slot use: producer `push` once at startup (literal) or\nwhen its single invocation completes (single-push wire). All\nconsumer tasks `peek` to read the value as many times as their box\nruns. The cell is never empty after the initial push.\n\nN-cell pop slot use: producers `push` repeatedly. Consumer tasks\n`pop` one cell each. For tagged slots, `pop` returns the\nlowest-tag cell; for untagged, FIFO. Pop on an empty slot is a\nbug — the spawn rule guarantees the slot is non-empty before a\ntask spawns.\n\nThere is no `slot_ref` / `slot_unref` — slot lifetime is the run.\n\n## Submission timing\n\nTasks are spawned dynamically in response to slot pushes. Each box\nhas small per-box state used by the dispatch layer:\n\n```\nbox_runtime_state {\n    slot_id_t  *input_slots;     // one per input port (set at load)\n    int        *port_modes;      // PEEK or POP, per input port\n    int         n_inputs;\n    slot_id_t   counter_slot;    // iterator only: SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER slot;\n                                 // 0 / unused otherwise\n};\n```\n\nThe spawning rule:\n- When a producer pushes to one of a box's input slots, the\n  dispatch layer checks **does every input slot have a value\n  available?** \"Available\" means:\n  - For peek-mode (1-cell) slots: cell has been written at least\n    once. Once a peek slot is filled, it stays available — every\n    subsequent spawn-check on this box passes the peek-port check.\n  - For pop-mode (N-cell) slots: queue is non-empty.\n- If yes, spawn a `dispatch_task_t` and submit to the pool. The\n  task pops (or peeks) one value from each input slot when it\n  runs.\n- Each push that completes the input set triggers exactly one\n  spawn. Multiple pushes accumulate in pop slots; each pop\n  consumes one, and if more remain, the next push (or check)\n  re-fires the spawn rule.\n\nThis makes the pool's queue the rate buffer: pushes accumulate\nin pop slots (possibly multiple per slot), and one task per\naccumulated value gets spawned.\n\nTasks never block on slots. They're spawned after inputs are\nready, run to completion, and disappear. Blocking-and-waking\nmachinery is unnecessary — the spawn-on-arrival rule is the\nsynchronization primitive.\n\nThe pool's queue is the only queue. There is no separate \"blocked\ntasks\" structure.\n\n## Allocation strategy: size-class free lists with coalescing fallback\n\nThe slot store uses a segregated free-list allocator. The map is\nanalyzed at compile time to enumerate every distinct slot size the\ngraph will need (each call box declares its output slot size; each\nqueued-input ring declares its total size from cell capacity × queue\ndepth). The allocator builds one free list per distinct size class.\n\nVariable-size and unknown-size payloads (a long LLM response, an\narray whose length is not known until runtime) are handled by a\nseparate **large-value heap** described below — not by allocating\nhuge slots up front.\n\n### The lists\nEach size class is an array (or linked list) of free slots of exactly\nthat size. At startup, each list is pre-populated with enough slots\nto cover the static box count for that size. Lists grow during the\nrun if demand exceeds the pre-allocation.\n\nEach list has its own mutex — allocation and deallocation in different\nsize classes never contend with each other.\n\n### Allocation\nGiven a request for size N bytes:\n1. Find the smallest size class with `class_size ≥ N`.\n2. If that class has a free slot, pop it. Done.\n3. Otherwise, try the next larger size class. Repeat.\n4. If a larger class hits, the slot is oversized for the request.\n   Try to slice the unused tail into a residual slot. If the residual\n   is at least as large as the smallest size class, push it onto that\n   class's list. Otherwise skip the slice — oversize the allocation\n   and live with the waste until the slot is freed.\n5. If no size class has a free slot, attempt to coalesce: walk the\n   address-ordered chunk list looking for adjacent free chunks that\n   together meet the requested size. If found, merge them and return\n   the combined chunk.\n6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and\n   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.\n7. After steps 5 or 6 complete, queue a deferred cleanup task on the\n   pool. Cleanup runs on a worker thread later and walks the\n   chunk list to opportunistically coalesce contiguous free chunks\n   into the largest possible chunks. Cleanup is best-effort — it\n   does not block any other thread. If memory fragments faster than\n   cleanup can keep up, the next allocation grows the heap; that's\n   fine.\n\n### Deallocation\nWhen refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's\nfree list. The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:\ncheck the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge\nthem and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.\nThis is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps\nsmall-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred\ncleanup task to run.\n\n### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)\nCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in\nmemory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.\n\nTwo viable representations:\n\n- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in\n  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.\n  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.\n- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start\n  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and\n  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to\n  scan.\n\nThe linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for\nsplits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows\nlist traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary\nindex — the API doesn't change.\n\n### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)\n\nFor values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM\nresponses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound\nis not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value\ndirectly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:\n\n```\n{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }\n```\n\n`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a\nplain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.\nWhen a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.\n2. Writes the bytes there.\n3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.\n\nThe consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,\ncopies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's\nrefcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the\nlarge-value-heap region.\n\nThe slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.\nThe two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still\nsupporting unbounded outputs.\n\nA box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as\n\"variable-size\" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the\nfixed-size path with no indirection.\n\n### Growth\nWhen all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy\na request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,\ndividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class\nlists. Plain heap memory is fine — no spec needs cross-process access\nto slot memory.\n\n### Why this design\n- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single\n  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.\n- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the\n  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply\n  not split.\n- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,\n  and it costs nothing on the common path.\n- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never\n  fires.\n\n## No type tags\n\nSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\nreads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\non each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\ncompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\nbuild time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not\nneed to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything\nelse. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Core milestone — 2026-05-12\n\nWhat shipped:\n- `src/009-slot-store.h` — the public API exactly as the design\n  describes: `slot_alloc` / `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop` /\n  `slot_read_inc` / `slot_has_value` / `slot_fill_count`. Plus the\n  store lifecycle pair and a small inspection helper for tests.\n- `src/009-slot-store.c` — implementation. Plain-malloc per slot\n  (size-class free lists deferred); ring slots and atomic-counter\n  slots both supported; the SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED variant of pop scans\n  for the lowest-tag filled cell. Per-slot spinlock via\n  `atomic_flag`. Atomic counter via `atomic_fetch_add_explicit`,\n  no lock.\n- `tests/009-slot-store-test.c` — 12 unit tests covering peek\n  semantics, FIFO pop, tagged pop ordering (in-order and\n  interleaved), atomic counter (sequential + 8-thread concurrent),\n  bad-argument paths, ring-full / empty edge cases, and a\n  multi-thread producer/consumer race over 5000 values.\n- Makefile additions: `test` target builds test binaries via a\n  pattern rule and runs them. Per-test prerequisites listed\n  explicitly so each binary links the minimal set of source `.o`s.\n- File index counter advanced to `009`.\n\nVerified clean build and 12/12 tests pass in `make STRICT=1`\n(`-Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic`).\n\nWhat's deferred to a follow-on within 302:\n- **Size-class free lists with coalescing.** The current\n  implementation `malloc`s each slot independently. That's correct\n  but unoptimized. Slots are allocated once at graph load and never\n  freed until run end, so under the current usage pattern free-list\n  reuse buys nothing. Lands once profiling justifies it (or once\n  long-running maps surface allocation pressure).\n- **Large-value heap for variable-size payloads.** Slots currently\n  store fixed-size cells; very large outputs (multi-MB LLM\n  responses, dynamically-sized arrays) will need the two-tier\n  scheme described under \"Large-value heap\" above. Blocks no\n  in-flight phase 3 work until a graph wants variable-size outputs.\n\nNeither deferred item blocks 301 / 304 / 305 / 306 / 307 / 308.\n\n### Large-value heap milestone — 2026-05-19\n\nThe variable-size payload follow-on landed in two layers:\n\n1. **`src/015-large-value-heap.{c,h}`** — chunked arena allocator.\n   Default 64 KB chunks; oversized allocations (larger than the\n   default chunk) get their own exact-fit chunk so one large value\n   doesn't bloat the regular bump chunks. Pointer stability is the\n   load-bearing property: chunks never move once allocated, so a\n   consumer's pointer survives any number of subsequent producer\n   allocations. Eight unit tests in\n   `tests/015-large-value-heap-test.c` cover the create/destroy\n   round-trip, single + multi alloc within a chunk, oversized\n   allocations getting their own chunks, pointer stability across\n   forced growth, zero-size allocations returning non-NULL, the\n   stats accessors, and an eight-thread / eight-thousand-alloc\n   concurrency stress test that asserts every returned pointer is\n   unique and writable.\n\n2. **Slot-store integration.** Added `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` to\n   `slot_alloc`. Cell layout for LARGE_VALUE slots is\n   `filled_size (4 bytes) + pad/tag (4 bytes) + stable pointer\n   (8 bytes)` — the 8-byte payload offset keeps the pointer\n   naturally aligned regardless of whether SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED is\n   also set. The slot store lazy-creates one shared lvh heap on\n   the first LARGE_VALUE allocation; the heap is destroyed\n   alongside the store. Push allocates from the heap *outside*\n   the slot spinlock (the heap has its own mutex; nesting is\n   fine, but reducing time-under-spinlock keeps the lock fast for\n   other producers). Peek and pop follow the cell's pointer and\n   memcpy the requested bytes back into the caller's buffer.\n\nFour new slot-store tests cover the new path:\n`large_value_push_pop` (100 KB payload, double-peek, then pop);\n`large_value_buf_too_small` (oversized payload + small dest →\n-1, cell preserved); `large_value_multi_push_fifo` (three\ndifferent-size values pushed and popped in order); and\n`large_value_tagged_ordering` (LARGE_VALUE + TAGGED → pops\nreturn lowest-tag-first with bytes intact).\n\nWhat this unblocks: any box that wants to emit a variable-size\noutput can now declare its downstream consumer slots with\nSLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE and produce payloads whose size isn't\nknown at graph-load time. The wiring from declared box output\ntype to the LARGE_VALUE flag in `graph_attach_runtime` lands as\na follow-on once a fixture or real graph requires it; the\nfoundation is in place.\n\n### Producer-driven LARGE_VALUE wiring — 2026-05-19\n\nThe \"wiring from declared box output type\" deferred above is\nnow in place. During `graph_attach_runtime`, each consumer\ninput slot's flags get OR'd with `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` if any\nproducer feeding that port declares `output_capacity == 0`. The\nrule covers both data boxes (which default to 0 because the\nfield isn't in their JSON schema) and call boxes that opt into\nvariable-size output by setting `\"output_capacity\": 0`. A\nmixed-language fan-in where any producer is variable-size\nupgrades the whole slot to LARGE_VALUE — the conservative call,\nsince the slot can only carry one format and the LVH path\nhandles small payloads correctly too.\n\nA new test in `tests/010-graph-loader-test.c`\n(`variable_size_producer_lvh_wiring`) attaches the hello fixture\nwith a deliberately tight default_cell_bytes of 512, then\nasserts a 2 KB push succeeds on greet's `name` port (fed by\ndata box `who`) and fails on greet's `salutation` port (literal\nonly, no producer). The discriminator is the slot's capacity:\nwithout LARGE_VALUE the 2 KB push exceeds 512 and is rejected;\nwith it the heap absorbs the bytes and the push lands.\n\nThe remaining phase-3 checklist item \"Variable-size outputs\nwork via the large-value heap\" is now satisfied end-to-end at\nthe slot-store boundary. A graph fixture that exercises the\npath on the dispatch side — a Lua box returning a multi-KB\nstring and a downstream box reading it — is a one-line fixture\naddition and lands with the 6-more-integration-fixtures task.\n\nWhat's still deferred within 302:\n- **Size-class free lists with coalescing.** Still no need.\n- **Per-allocation free in the large-value heap.** The heap\n  grows monotonically for the life of a run. Long-running\n  iterator loops that emit large values will pin memory until\n  run end. Acceptable for current fixtures; a size-class\n  allocator with eager-coalesce is the upgrade path if profiling\n  flags it.\n",

{

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Yes, that design exists in the project. Written down, partially built, partially still a sketch. Let me try to lay it out without jumping between names.\n\nThere are actually two separate memory systems that get tangled together in casual talk. Worth pulling them apart first.\n\n**The first system** is for values whose maximum size is known before the run starts. This is the case the design you're remembering was written for. The plan, exactly as you described it: before the run begins, the loader walks the entire graph and lists every distinct value-size that will ever be needed. For each distinct size it builds a separate free-list, pre-populated with enough entries to cover every place in the graph that needs that size. Asking for a value of size N becomes \"find the right list, pop one\" — no searching, no walks. Giving one back puts it on the same list. The give-back step also peeks at the slot's two physical neighbors in memory; if either neighbor is also free, they merge into one bigger free chunk that goes onto the appropriate larger-size list. On top of all that, a background sweep runs from time to time, walking the whole region opportunistically merging anything that's contiguous and free.\n\nThat's the design in full. What's actually in the codebase is much simpler: at startup, the system just asks the operating system for memory one slot at a time and never returns it. The size-class lists and the neighbor-merging — both deferred. The reasoning written into the project is that for the maps the editor produces today, every value lives the whole run anyway, so there's nothing to reclaim and the simple version is fine.\n\n**The second system** is for values whose size isn't known until they're produced. Long text from an LLM, arrays whose length depends on input — anything where the graph can't write down an upper bound. These values don't sit directly in their value slots. Instead, the slot holds a tiny handle (size + pointer), and the actual bytes live in a separate pool.\n\nThat separate pool is the thing the developer asking the question cares about, because it's where the long LLM responses on their multi-day runs would accumulate. Today, that pool is dead simple: a chain of fixed-size blocks. When a producer wants to store bytes, it appends to the current block; when the current block doesn't have room, a new one gets allocated; if a value is bigger than a normal block, it gets its own custom-sized block. **Nothing is ever returned to the system mid-run.** The pool grows monotonically until the run ends, at which point the whole thing is freed in one piece.\n\nThere's a note attached to the implementation that says, near-verbatim: this grows monotonically, long-running loops that emit large values will pin memory until run-end, acceptable for current fixtures, and the upgrade path is the size-class allocator with eager-coalesce — the same design as the first system. So both systems point at the same upgrade, neither has built it.\n\n**Now — to answer their actual question.**\n\nThe design they want (chunk-size enumeration, free on last reference, eager-merge on free, background sweep) is the explicit upgrade path spelled out for both memory systems. It hasn't been built on either side. There's no roadmap commitment to building it soon, because the maps that exist today don't trigger the problem.\n\nA subtle but important wrinkle: \"free on last reference\" requires actually knowing when the last reference is gone. The current system uses lifetime-of-run as a stand-in for reference counting, because that's free — when the run ends, everyone's done with everything. Switching to actual reference counts means touching every place that hands out a pointer to a stored value to make it bump and drop the count. That's a wider change than just the allocator. So when they're weighing wait-vs-build, the real cost isn't writing a size-class allocator (that's a few hundred lines of textbook code) — the real cost is wiring reference counting through the dispatch layer that hands values from producer to consumer.\n\nIf I were the developer asking this question, my read would be:\n- Waiting means waiting for someone here to hit the same problem, and the runs here are short, so that may never happen on its own.\n- Building it themselves is implementing a design that's already written down, which means the work isn't speculative. But it includes the reference-counting infrastructure, not just the allocator.\n- There's a third option worth flagging: keep the monotonic allocator but make the runtime checkpoint-and-restart. Every few hours, drain in-flight work, dump live state, restart the process. Skips the whole memory-reclamation question. Whether that fits their workload depends on whether their runs can tolerate brief pauses.\n\nWant me to put any of this into a file for the other developer, or is this for you to relay?"
      }],

If\n17\tanother process — a long-running runner, a different shell, a\n18\tsibling tool that opened the artifact yesterday — had pinned to\n19\tthat exact compiled layout (a particular `pool-runner` binary, a\n20\tparticular `spec.so` ABI, a particular set of pre-compiled C\n21\tboxes), the rebuild yanks the rug. Other\n32\tprograms that depend on a particular build of a map are expected\n33\tto *acquire* a reference on startup and *release* it on shutdown.\n34\tWhen `soramech-compile` is asked to rebuild a map that has any\n35\tlive references, it does NOT clobber the existing directory.\n36\tInstead it builds a sibling directory next door, leaving the\n37\treferenced one untouched until its holders are done with it.\n38\t\n39\tThe reference count is **expected to be unreliable**. A crashing\n40\tholder doesn't get the chance to release; an SSH session that\n41\tdrops doesn't either. The design accepts that staleness is the\n42\tcommon case, not the exception — every reference entry carries\n43\tenough metadata to be independently validated and (eventually)\n44\treaped. The reference count is a hint and a courtesy, not a\n45\tguarantee.\n46\t\n47\tThis is conceptually a copy-on-write filesystem for compiled\n48\tartifacts: writes (rebuilds) fork the universe when readers\n49\texist; readers can keep reading the version they pinned to;\n50\tgenerations get garbage-collected when nothing observable still\n51\tpoints at them.\n52\t\n53\t## Concept\n54\t\n55\tA compiled directory contains a `.refs` file (hidden, dot-prefixed\n56\tso it doesn't clutter directory listings). It's append-only by\n57\tdesign — concurrent acquires never need to take a lock; concurrent\n58\treleases write a separate marker without rewriting the file.\n59\t\n60\tEach reference has three parts:\n61\t\n62\t1. **A date.** When the reference was acquired. Lets a janitor\n63\t   prune references older than some threshold even if their back\n64\t   pointer can't be validated.\n65\t2. **A back-pointer.** The identity of the holder — enough\n66\t   information that an outside observer can ask \"is this holder\n67\t   still alive, and does it still want this reference?\" without\n68\t   trusting the count alone. Concrete candidates:\n69\t   - process PID + start time (PID alone is not enough; PIDs\n70\t     recycle)\n71\t   - a path to a marker file the holder maintains (presence of\n72\t     the marker = the holder is still live and aware of the\n73\t     ref)\n74\t   - some combination (PID + a marker path)\n75\t3. **An opaque ref id.** A short string the holder can use later\n76\t   to identify *its* reference when it wants to release, so it\n77\t   doesn't accidentally release someone else's.\n78\t\n79\tA release writes an entry referencing the original acquire id.\n80\tNet live refs = acquires whose id isn't in the release set.\n81\t\n82\t## Reference file format\n83\t\n84\tA line-oriented log. Each line is one of two record types:\n85\t\n86\t```\n87\tacquire <id> <iso8601-date> <pid> <pid-start-time-ticks> <marker-path>\n88\trelease <id> <iso8601-date>\n89\t```\n90\t\n91\tAppend-only. Holders open with `O_APPEND` and write a single line\n92\tper operation. Atomic on POSIX as long as the line fits in\n93\t`PIPE_BUF` (4 KB on Linux) — well within budget for these short\n94\trecords.\n95\t\n96\tReading: tail through the file, build a set of acquire ids,\n97\tsubtract release ids; remaining ids are nominally live. Then\n98\tvalidate each survivor's back pointer.\n99\t\n100\tA `.refs.lock` file is used only for compaction (rewriting the\n101\tlog to drop matched acquire/release pairs) and for the\n102\tfork-to-sibling decision during compile. Steady-state reads /\n103\twrites don't lock.\n104\t\n105\t## Acquire / release API\n106\t\n107\tA small helper utility, probably a shell script for portability\n108\tsince holders are written in many languages:\n109\t\n110\t```\n111\tscripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir> [--id <id>] [--marker <path>]\n112\tscripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>\n113\tscripts/soramech-ref.sh list    <compiled-dir>          # JSON, including staleness verdicts\n114\tscripts/soramech-ref.sh reap    <compiled-dir>          # compact + drop dead refs\n115\t```\n116\t\n117\t`acquire` prints the assigned id to stdout; the holder is\n118\tresponsible for plumbing it to wherever it'll need to call\n119\trelease. If no `--id` was supplied, the script generates one\n120\t(timestamp + random suffix).\n121\t\n122\t`list` walks the log and prints a JSON array of `{id, date,\n123\tholder, valid}` entries. Validation reads the back pointer's\n124\tliveness signal (PID exists & start-time matches, or marker file\n125\texists).\n126\t\n127\t`reap` is destructive — it rewrites the log to remove entries\n128\twhose holders failed validation. Run periodically; never\n129\tautomatically as part of compile (compile must not destroy state\n130\tits caller might care about).\n131\t\n132\t## Compile-time fork logic\n133\t\n134\t`soramech-compile.sh` consults `<map>/compiled/.refs` (and any\n135\tsibling generation directories' `.refs` files) before deciding\n136\twhere to write:\n137\t\n138\t1. If `<map>/compiled/` doesn't exist → build there, fresh.\n139\t2. If it exists but has zero live references → build there, after\n140\t   `rm -rf`. Same destructive behavior as today.\n141\t3. If it exists with one or more live references → pick a sibling\n142\t   directory name (see below) and build there. The original\n143\t   `compiled/` stays intact.\n144\t\n145\tAfter a fork-build, the caller has a new directory; `manifest.json`\n146\tin the new directory records the fork relationship (`forked_from`\n147\tfield pointing at the previous generation's path).\n148\t\n149\t### Sibling directory naming\n150\t\n151\tTwo reasonable schemes; pick whichever the implementer prefers:\n152\t\n153\t- **Generation index:** `compiled.0`, `compiled.1`, `compiled.2`...\n154\t  Always pick `compiled.N` where N is one more than the highest\n155\t  existing generation. Easy to grep for; index order = build\n156\t  order.\n157\t- **Timestamp suffix:** `compiled.2026-05-19T2347` (ISO 8601\n158\t  compact). Order-preserving lexicographically; the name itself\n159\t  tells the operator when it was built.\n160\t\n161\tWhichever wins, the script should also leave a `compiled` symlink\n162\tpointing at the newest generation, so callers who want \"the\n163\tlatest\" don't have to enumerate.\n164\t\n165\t## Stale reference handling\n166\t\n167\tA reference is stale if any of the following hold:\n168\t\n169\t- The PID no longer exists on the system.\n170\t- The PID exists but its start time (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22)\n171\t  doesn't match the recorded value — different process, recycled\n172\t  PID.\n173\t- The marker file path was supplied at acquire and is now\n174\t  missing.\n175\t\n176\tStale refs are *tolerated*: compile-time fork still triggers if\n177\tANY ref exists, stale or otherwise — the caller can run\n178\t`soramech-ref.sh reap` first if they want to consolidate. The\n179\tphilosophy is: the artifact directory belongs to its readers\n180\tuntil proven otherwise, and the cost of an extra build dir is\n181\ttrivial compared to the cost of a use-after-rebuild crash.\n182\t\n183\t## Gitignore considerations\n184\t\n185\tEvery generation (`compiled/`, `compiled.0/`, `compiled.1/`,\n186\t`compiled.2026-05-19T2347/`, the `compiled` symlink) is a derived\n187\tartifact and should never be tracked. Pick the back-pointer format. Recommend PID + start time +\n202\t   optional marker path. Document the choice with a comment at\n203\t   the top of the ref helper.\n204\t2. Write `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` with `acquire`, `release`,\n205\t   `list`, `reap`. Append-only writes for the first two, log\n206\t   rewrite under `.refs.lock` for the last.\n207\t3. Add a small `tests/315-refs-test.sh` that exercises:\n208\t   acquire → list (1 entry, valid) → release → list (0 valid) →\n209\t   acquire → kill the holder process → list (1 entry, stale) →\n210\t   reap → list (0).\n211\t4. Teach `soramech-compile.sh` to read `.refs` and pick the\n212\t   target directory. Implement the sibling-naming scheme.\n213\t   `compiled` becomes a symlink to the newest generation.\n214\t5. Add a `forked_from` field to `manifest.json` when forking.\n215\t6. Update `.gitignore` for the new generation pattern.\n216\t7. On the one hand, yes —\n225\t  it's the canonical case the system protects against. On the\n226\t  other, soramech-pool runs are usually short-lived and the\n227\t  acquire/release overhead per run is unwelcome. If `compiled.5` is built while\n230\t  `compiled.4` had live refs but `compiled.4`'s refs are now all\n231\t  stale (caller never released, then died), do we ever prune\n232\t  `compiled.4`? A reliable reference\n258\tcount would require a kernel-level mechanism (file locks held\n259\tfor the lifetime of the holder), and that's a tower of\n260\toperational complexity for marginal value. By accepting that\n261\tholders sometimes lie and sometimes vanish, we get a system\n262\tthat's robust to crashes, network drops, and SIGKILL — at the\n263\tcost of needing a \"reap\" pass to catch up with reality\n264\toccasionally. The back pointer is what makes that catch-up\n265\tpossible: it's the bridge between what the log claims and what\n266\tthe world actually shows.\n267\t\n268\tA reference is a wish, not a contract. Concrete candidates:\n   - process PID + start time (PID alone is not enough; PIDs\n     recycle)\n   - a path to a marker file the holder maintains (presence of\n     the marker = the holder is still live and aware of the\n     ref)\n   - some combination (PID + a marker path)\n3. **An opaque ref id.** A short string the holder can use later\n   to identify *its* reference when it wants to release, so it\n   doesn't accidentally release someone else's.\n\nA release writes an entry referencing the original acquire id.\nNet live refs = acquires whose id isn't in the release set.\n\n## Reference file format\n\nA line-oriented log. Each line is one of two record types:\n\n```\nacquire <id> <iso8601-date> <pid> <pid-start-time-ticks> <marker-path>\nrelease <id> <iso8601-date>\n```\n\nAppend-only. Holders open with `O_APPEND` and write a single line\nper operation. Atomic on POSIX as long as the line fits in\n`PIPE_BUF` (4 KB on Linux) — well within budget for these short\nrecords.\n\nReading: tail through the file, build a set of acquire ids,\nsubtract release ids; remaining ids are nominally live. Then\nvalidate each survivor's back pointer.\n\nA `.refs.lock` file is used only for compaction (rewriting the\nlog to drop matched acquire/release pairs) and for the\nfork-to-sibling decision during compile. Steady-state reads /\nwrites don't lock.\n\n## Acquire / release API\n\nA small helper utility, probably a shell script for portability\nsince holders are written in many languages:\n\n```\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir> [--id <id>] [--marker <path>]\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh list    <compiled-dir>          # JSON, including staleness verdicts\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh reap    <compiled-dir>          # compact + drop dead refs\n```\n\n`acquire` prints the assigned id to stdout; the holder is\nresponsible for plumbing it to wherever it'll need to call\nrelease. If no `--id` was supplied, the script generates one\n(timestamp + random suffix).\n\n`list` walks the log and prints a JSON array of `{id, date,\nholder, valid}` entries. Validation reads the back pointer's\nliveness signal (PID exists & start-time matches, or marker file\nexists).\n\n`reap` is destructive — it rewrites the log to remove entries\nwhose holders failed validation. Run periodically; never\nautomatically as part of compile (compile must not destroy state\nits caller might care about).\n\n## Compile-time fork logic\n\n`soramech-compile.sh` consults `<map>/compiled/.refs` (and any\nsibling generation directories' `.refs` files) before deciding\nwhere to write:\n\n1. If `<map>/compiled/` doesn't exist → build there, fresh.\n2. If it exists but has zero live references → build there, after\n   `rm -rf`. Same destructive behavior as today.\n3. If it exists with one or more live references → pick a sibling\n   directory name (see below) and build there. The original\n   `compiled/` stays intact.\n\nAfter a fork-build, the caller has a new directory; `manifest.json`\nin the new directory records the fork relationship (`forked_from`\nfield pointing at the previous generation's path).\n\n### Sibling directory naming\n\nTwo reasonable schemes; pick whichever the implementer prefers:\n\n- **Generation index:** `compiled.0`, `compiled.1`, `compiled.2`...\n  Always pick `compiled.N` where N is one more than the highest\n  existing generation. Easy to grep for; index order = build\n  order.\n- **Timestamp suffix:** `compiled.2026-05-19T2347` (ISO 8601\n  compact). Order-preserving lexicographically; the name itself\n  tells the operator when it was built.\n\nWhichever wins, the script should also leave a `compiled` symlink\npointing at the newest generation, so callers who want \"the\nlatest\" don't have to enumerate.\n\n## Stale reference handling\n\nA reference is stale if any of the following hold:\n\n- The PID no longer exists on the system.\n- The PID exists but its start time (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22)\n  doesn't match the recorded value — different process, recycled\n  PID.\n- The marker file path was supplied at acquire and is now\n  missing.\n\nStale refs are *tolerated*: compile-time fork still triggers if\nANY ref exists, stale or otherwise — the caller can run\n`soramech-ref.sh reap` first if they want to consolidate. The\nphilosophy is: the artifact directory belongs to its readers\nuntil proven otherwise, and the cost of an extra build dir is\ntrivial compared to the cost of a use-after-rebuild crash.\n\n## Gitignore considerations\n\nEvery generation (`compiled/`, `compiled.0/`, `compiled.1/`,\n`compiled.2026-05-19T2347/`, the `compiled` symlink) is a derived\nartifact and should never be tracked. The existing\n`.gitignore` line `tests/maps/*/compiled/` covers the canonical\nname; add a sibling pattern to cover generations:\n\n```\ntests/maps/*/compiled/\ntests/maps/*/compiled.*/\n```\n\nThe `.refs` file itself lives *inside* the compiled directory,\nso it inherits the same gitignore.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Pick the back-pointer format. Recommend PID + start time +\n   optional marker path. Document the choice with a comment at\n   the top of the ref helper.\n2. Write `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` with `acquire`, `release`,\n   `list`, `reap`. Append-only writes for the first two, log\n   rewrite under `.refs.lock` for the last.\n3. Add a small `tests/315-refs-test.sh` that exercises:\n   acquire → list (1 entry, valid) → release → list (0 valid) →\n   acquire → kill the holder process → list (1 entry, stale) →\n   reap → list (0).\n4. Teach `soramech-compile.sh` to read `.refs` and pick the\n   target directory. Implement the sibling-naming scheme.\n   `compiled` becomes a symlink to the newest generation.\n5. Add a `forked_from` field to `manifest.json` when forking.\n6. Update `.gitignore` for the new generation pattern.\n7. Integration check in `scripts/run-tests.sh`: compile the\n   pipeline fixture twice — second time with a live `acquire` —\n   assert a sibling generation was created and the original\n   pinned generation still runs unchanged.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Should the runner (`soramech-pool`) itself acquire a reference\n  when it opens a compiled directory? On the one hand, yes —\n  it's the canonical case the system protects against. On the\n  other, soramech-pool runs are usually short-lived and the\n  acquire/release overhead per run is unwelcome. Possible\n  compromise: only acquire if pool runs longer than N seconds.\n- How does a fork chain end? If `compiled.5` is built while\n  `compiled.4` had live refs but `compiled.4`'s refs are now all\n  stale (caller never released, then died), do we ever prune\n  `compiled.4`? Probably yes, via `soramech-ref.sh reap-all\n  <map>` which walks every generation and drops the ones whose\n  refs all validate as dead.\n- Is the `.refs` log itself something that should be versioned\n  (`.refs.v1`)? If we ever change the line format, in-flight\n  holders won't know how to read it. Versioning the filename\n  avoids the problem.\n- Does the editor (`maps/<x>/` user-facing) want the same\n  mechanism? Probably yes eventually, but out of scope for this\n  issue — start with `compiled/` artifacts only.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — issue 309's compile pipeline,\n  modified here to fork on live references\n- `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` — new helper for acquire / release /\n  list / reap\n- `tests/315-refs-test.sh` — new\n- `.gitignore` — extended pattern for generation directories\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — new integration check\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — parent issue; references this\n  one's fork behavior\n\n## Notes (philosophy)\n\nThe unreliability is a feature, not a bug. A reliable reference\ncount would require a kernel-level mechanism (file locks held\nfor the lifetime of the holder), and that's a tower of\noperational complexity for marginal value. By accepting that\nholders sometimes lie and sometimes vanish, we get a system\nthat's robust to crashes, network drops, and SIGKILL — at the\ncost of needing a \"reap\" pass to catch up with reality\noccasionally. The back pointer is what makes that catch-up\npossible: it's the bridge between what the log claims and what\nthe world actually shows.\n\nA reference is a wish, not a contract. The compile pipeline\nhonors wishes by default and only stops honoring them when\nnothing in the world supports the wish anymore. That's how\nrespectful software treats its peers.\n",
      "startLine":1,

        "text":"You're right — I underread the file. The comprehensive design is there. Let me walk through what's actually written down, because it's better than I made it sound.\n\n**Where it lives:** the file that covers how values flow from one box to another describes the memory side in detail. That's the issue file I was reading from in my previous answer — I just stopped at the implementation-log notes and didn't relay the design that sits above them. My fault.\n\n**What the comprehensive design actually says:**\n\nBefore the run starts, the loader looks at the whole graph and writes down every distinct value-size that's going to be needed. For each distinct size it makes a separate free-list. Asking for a value of size N becomes \"go to the right list, pop one.\" Giving it back puts it on the same list.\n\nTwo things happen on the give-back step that I left out the first time around:\n\nThe first is the cheap merge. When a chunk goes back to its list, the deallocator looks at the two chunks physically next to it in memory. If either one is also free, the three chunks (or two) get fused into one bigger chunk, which then goes onto the list for the bigger size. This means the typical fragmentation pattern — lots of small holes scattered around — never builds up, because adjacent holes immediately become one big hole.\n\nThe second is the deferred sweep. Periodically, a background pass walks the whole region looking for runs of adjacent free chunks and merges anything it finds. Best-effort; doesn't block anyone. Catches the cases where the cheap merge couldn't fire because of timing.\n\nBoth of those steps assume that \"give back\" is a real event that actually happens. That's where the system relies on reference counting — when the last consumer of a value is done, the count hits zero and that's the signal to give the chunk back.\n\n**Where I gave you a wrong impression:** I said the slot system uses lifetime-of-run as a stand-in for reference counting. That's true of what's *actually running today*, but the design as written does spell out the refcount-and-merge story — I read past it. The reason the running code doesn't exercise it is just that nothing currently frees mid-run, so the deallocator never fires. The plumbing exists in the design; it's the \"real signal that something is done\" that isn't being generated.\n\n**Your reuse question, which is the actually important one:**\n\nYes. That's exactly the right move and I should have led with it.\n\nThe pattern you're describing — count references, free when the count hits zero, merge adjacent free regions back into usable memory, replenish from a pool sized to expected demand — is one pattern, not two. The design file describes it for the fixed-size value pipeline. The variable-size value region (the thing the other developer is worried about) is the same shape of problem: chunks of memory get used, some held by one consumer, some held by many, and they need to come back when nobody needs them.\n\nThere's no reason these should be separate systems. The variable-size region's current implementation — a simple chain of blocks that never gives anything back — is the kind of thing you write when you haven't decided yet what the real allocator looks like. It was honest as a placeholder; it's not appropriate as a long-term answer for the reasons you said. Calling it a memory leak by design is fair.\n\nWhat the project should do, in plain terms:\n\nBuild one allocator. It looks at the graph beforehand, makes a list of every value-size that's going to appear, and stands up a free-list per size. Every value handed out is reference-counted by whoever holds it. When the last holder drops their reference, the chunk goes back to its list, with the eager-merge step checking neighbors. A background sweep occasionally walks the whole thing to catch larger merges.\n\nThis allocator serves both purposes. The fixed-size value pipeline uses it. The variable-size region uses it. They're not different stores with different policies — they're one store, and the only thing that changes is whether the value's size came from the graph upfront or showed up at runtime.\n\nThe reference-counting wiring is the cost you'd pay either way. Every place that hands out a pointer to a stored value would need to bump the count when handing it out and drop it when the consumer is done. That's the part that touches a lot of code — not because the change in any one place is hard, but because there are a lot of places. But you only do it once, and it covers both regions.\n\nSo my recommendation, since you asked: yes, design it as one system, modeled on the slot allocator's reference-and-merge design as already written down. Don't write a second design for the variable-size region. The instinct that the project keeps re-creating patterns is correct — this is one of those moments where catching it pays off. And the existing design isn't being thrown away; it's being implemented for real for the first time, and applied uniformly instead of in one half of the system.\n\nWant me to update the relevant issue file to reflect that this is now one allocator covering both cases, rather than two with one deferred?"

There is no per-slot reference\ncounting and no end-of-stream propagation — the slot is freed\nwhen the run ends, alongside its owning box.\n\nRun termination is governed entirely by the pool's active-task\ncounter (issue 301): when no task is running and no further spawns\nare pending, the run is over. A slot that has no value yet simply means the\nspawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,\nno per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\nper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\nhands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\nsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\nit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n\nSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\nheader mutations. There is no allocator-wide mutex on the\nread/write path; only the per-size-class free lists in the\nallocator have their own locks.\n\n## Slot creation\n",

## [348]

```json
{
  "isSidechain":false,
  "timestamp":"2026-05-20T00:40:03.414Z",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "sessionId":"1d15fc56-aebf-4306-867c-c2ae6b792f2d",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"**On how the loader knows sizes:**\n\nThe graph itself carries the answer for the known cases. Every box that produces a value writes down — in its metadata — what size its output is going to be. A box that always emits a 32-byte number declares 32. A box that builds a 4-megabyte image and knows it does, declares 4 megabytes. The loader reads every one of these declarations before the run starts, deduplicates them, and uses that list to set up its pre-warmed pools.\n\nFor the unknown case — an LLM call where the response could be 100 bytes or 100 kilobytes, a dynamic array whose length depends on input — the box just declares \"size not known.\" When the loader sees that, it doesn't pre-warm a pool for that box; it knows the value will need to be allocated on demand when the box actually produces something.\n\nBoth kinds of value come out of the same underlying memory. The difference is just whether the loader had a pool ready for that size or not. A known-size value pops from its pre-warmed list — one step. An unknown-size value goes through a path that says \"find me the smallest free region that fits, slice it if needed, give me back the front.\" Same allocator, two doors. The unknown-size door is slightly slower per allocation, but that cost is dwarfed by whatever produced the value in the first place (the LLM call itself, the array construction).\n\nThe case you raised — known-at-compile-time large allocation — is fully covered by the first door. There's nothing special about \"large\" here. The free-list approach treats a 4-megabyte size class no differently than a 32-byte size class; just a different list.\n\n**On deterministic sweep triggers:**\n\nTwo natural moments. Both are decoupled from wall-clock time.\n\nThe first is the moment an allocation request can't be satisfied from any existing free-list. This is the obvious one — the system knows it's about to fail. Before it gives up and asks the operating system for more memory, it runs the sweep to consolidate any fragments that the cheap neighbor-merge didn't catch. If the sweep produces enough contiguous space to satisfy the request, the allocation succeeds and the heap doesn't grow. If it doesn't, only then does the system ask the OS for more. This makes the sweep the immediate alternative to heap growth — which is exactly when its work has the most value. It's also fully deterministic: same allocation pattern, same sweep moments.\n\nThe second is quiescence — moments when nothing is running. The runtime already recognizes these moments because it uses them to decide a run is complete. Between batches is a natural opportunity because no tasks are reading or writing chunks at that instant, so the sweep can be more aggressive without coordinating with anyone.\n\nI'd start with just the first. It's the mandatory one — it's what stands between \"allocation failed\" and \"ask the OS for more memory.\" The second is opportunistic and can be added later if profiling shows fragmentation is sneaking through.\n\nA third option just to name it: trigger the sweep when the count of small free fragments crosses a threshold (an obvious sign of splintering). Deterministic, but needs tuning the threshold, and the first option covers most of the same ground without that work.\n\nNow updating the file."
      }],

The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:\ncheck the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge\nthem and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.\nThis is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps\nsmall-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred\ncleanup task to run.\n\n### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)\nCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in\nmemory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.\n\nTwo viable representations:\n\n- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in\n  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.\n  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.\n- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start\n  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and\n  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to\n  scan.\n\nThe linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for\nsplits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows\nlist traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary\nindex — the API doesn't change.\n\n### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)\n\nFor values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM\nresponses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound\nis not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value\ndirectly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:\n\n```\n{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }\n```\n\n`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a\nplain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.\nWhen a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.\n2. Writes the bytes there.\n3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.\n\nThe consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,\ncopies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's\nrefcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the\nlarge-value-heap region.\n\nThe slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.\nThe two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still\nsupporting unbounded outputs.\n\nA box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as\n\"variable-size\" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the\nfixed-size path with no indirection.\n\n### Growth\nWhen all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy\na request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,\ndividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class\nlists. Plain heap memory is fine — no spec needs cross-process access\nto slot memory.\n\n### Why this design\n- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single\n  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.\n- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the\n  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply\n  not split.\n- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,\n  and it costs nothing on the common path.\n- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never\n  fires.",
          "new_string":"## Allocation strategy: one unified allocator for every value\n\nThere is one allocator. It serves both values whose size is known\nfrom the graph at compile time and values whose size only becomes\nknown when they're produced (LLM responses, dynamic arrays, anything\nwhere the upper bound isn't a useful number). The earlier draft of\nthis document split these into two stores — a size-class slot\nallocator for the known case, a separate \"large-value heap\" for the\nunknown case. That split was a mistake. They are the same problem\nand they reuse the same machinery; treating them as two stores led\nto the unknown-size path being a monotonically-growing pool that\nnever reclaims, which is a memory leak by design.\n\n### How the allocator learns sizes ahead of time\n\nBefore the run starts, the loader walks every box in the graph and\nreads the size that box declares for its output. A box that always\nproduces a 32-byte number declares 32. A box that always produces a\n4-megabyte image declares 4 megabytes. The loader collects every\ndistinct declared size, deduplicates them, and creates one free-list\nper distinct size. Each list is pre-populated with enough chunks to\ncover the static demand for that size.\n\nBoxes whose output size depends on runtime — the LLM case — declare\n\"size unknown.\" The loader doesn't create a pre-warmed list for those\nboxes; it knows their values will be allocated on demand.\n\nBoth kinds share the same underlying memory region. The difference is\nonly whether the loader had a list pre-warmed for the value's size.\n\n### Two doors, one allocator\n\n**Door 1 — declared-size allocation.** Given a request for size N,\nwhere N matches a declared size class: pop the head of that class's\nfree-list. One step. This is the common path for the vast majority\nof values; nearly every box in a typical graph has a declared output\nsize.\n\n**Door 2 — runtime-size allocation.** Given a request for an unknown\nsize at runtime: find the smallest size class whose chunks are large\nenough. If that class is exhausted, try the next-larger. If the\nchunk handed out is oversized for the request, slice the unused tail\ninto a residual chunk and push that residual onto the appropriate\nsmaller free-list. The residual is only kept if it's at least as large\nas the smallest declared size class — anything smaller is left as\ninternal waste rather than fragmenting the lists with stubs.\n\nBoth doors fall through to the same fragmentation-recovery and growth\nmachinery below when their free-lists can't satisfy a request.\n\n### Reference counting drives deallocation\n\nEvery value the allocator hands out is reference-counted. The dispatch\nlayer increments the count when handing a value to a consumer and\ndecrements it when the consumer is done. When the count reaches zero,\nthe chunk is returned to the allocator.\n\nThe return-to-allocator step does two things atomically: pushes the\nchunk onto the appropriate free-list AND checks the chunk's two\nphysical neighbors. If either neighbor is also free, the deallocator\nmerges them into a larger chunk and pushes the merged chunk onto the\nfree-list for the merged size. This eager neighbor-merge is O(1) and\nkeeps small-scale fragmentation from accumulating on the hot path.\n\nReference counting requires touching every place that hands out a\npointer to an allocator-managed value. That cost is paid once. After\nthe wiring exists, both doors above benefit from the same recycling.\n\n### When does the bigger sweep run\n\nThe eager neighbor-merge above catches the common case. It misses\npatterns where free chunks are scattered with allocated chunks between\nthem — the cheap merge can't see past its immediate neighbors.\n\nA deeper sweep that walks the whole address-ordered chunk list\nlooking for runs of contiguous free chunks runs on two deterministic\ntriggers, both decoupled from wall-clock time:\n\n1. **At the moment an allocation would otherwise fail.** When a\n   request can't be satisfied from any free-list — including after\n   trying larger classes and slicing — the system runs the deep sweep\n   before falling back to asking the operating system for more memory.\n   If the sweep produces a chunk large enough to satisfy the request,\n   the allocation succeeds and no growth happens. This is the\n   mandatory trigger: the sweep is the immediate alternative to\n   monotonic growth, and it fires exactly when its work has value.\n\n2. **At quiescence — moments when no task is running.** The dispatch\n   layer already recognizes these moments because it uses them to\n   decide a run is complete. Between batches is a natural opportunity\n   because no tasks are reading or writing chunks at that instant.\n   This is the opportunistic trigger.\n\nThe mandatory trigger is enough on its own. The opportunistic trigger\nis a tunable knob that can be enabled later if profiling shows\nfragmentation surviving the cheap merge faster than the mandatory\ntrigger catches up.\n\nA third option was considered — trigger when the count of small free\nfragments crosses a threshold — but rejected for now. It works, but\nit needs the threshold tuned, and the two triggers above cover the\nsame ground without that tuning step.\n\n### Physical-order chunk list (for the merge steps)\n\nBoth the eager neighbor-merge and the deeper sweep need to know\nwhich chunks are physically adjacent in memory. The size-class\nfree-lists don't carry that information — they're indexed by size,\nnot address.\n\nThe supporting structure is a doubly-linked list of all chunks (free\nand allocated) in address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given a\nchunk pointer. Neighbor lookup is O(1). The cost is pointer-chasing\nduring the deeper sweep, but the sweep only runs at the two triggers\nabove, not on the hot path.\n\nIf profiling later shows traversal cost hurting at sweep time, the\nlist can be swapped for a sorted-by-address array of `(start, end)`\npairs with an auxiliary index — the allocator's external API doesn't\nchange.\n\n### Why one allocator instead of two\n\nThe split design existed because the original two-tier scheme had a\n\"large-value heap\" carved out for variable-size payloads, on the\ntheory that mixing variable and fixed sizes in the same pool would\ncomplicate the fixed-size path. That reasoning doesn't survive\ncontact with reference counting and free-list recycling: with\nrefcount-driven free, the fixed-size path stays fast because most\nrequests match a declared class and pop in one step regardless of\nwhat else is in the region.\n\nSplitting them also meant the variable-size pool had to grow\nforever, because writing the same allocator twice — once with\nreclamation, once without — was more work than was budgeted in early\nphase 3. That's the position the current code is in. Unified gets us\nthe reclamation everywhere, with no extra design work.\n\n### Growth (last resort)\n\nWhen both doors fail and the deep sweep can't produce a fitting\nchunk, the allocator grows by asking the operating system for a new\nregion, dividing it into chunks per the declared size classes (or\ninto a single large chunk if the request was for an unknown size\nbeyond all declared classes), and threading the new chunks into the\nfree-lists and the address-ordered list.\n\nGrowth is the rare case. With pre-warmed free-lists sized to static\ndemand and refcount-driven recycling, a well-behaved graph never\nreaches growth — every allocation either pops a pre-warmed chunk or\nrecycles one whose last reference just dropped.",

If found, merge them and return","-   the combined chunk.","-6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and","-   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.","-7. After steps 5 or 6 complete, queue a deferred cleanup task on the","-   pool. Cleanup runs on a worker thread later and walks the","-   chunk list to opportunistically coalesce contiguous free chunks","-   into the largest possible chunks. Cleanup is best-effort — it","-   does not block any other thread. If memory fragments faster than","-   cleanup can keep up, the next allocation grows the heap; that's","-   fine.","+Both kinds share the same underlying memory region. The difference is","+only whether the loader had a list pre-warmed for the value's size."," ","-### Deallocation","-When refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's","-free list. The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:","-check the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge","-them and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.","-This is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps","-small-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred","-cleanup task to run.","+### Two doors, one allocator"," ","-### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)","-Coalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in","-memory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.","+**Door 1 — declared-size allocation.** Given a request for size N,","+where N matches a declared size class: pop the head of that class's","+free-list. One step. This is the common path for the vast majority","+of values; nearly every box in a typical graph has a declared output","+size."," ","-Two viable representations:","+**Door 2 — runtime-size allocation.** Given a request for an unknown","+size at runtime: find the smallest size class whose chunks are large","+enough. If that class is exhausted, try the next-larger. If the","+chunk handed out is oversized for the request, slice the unused tail","+into a residual chunk and push that residual onto the appropriate","+smaller free-list. The residual is only kept if it's at least as large","+as the smallest declared size class — anything smaller is left as","+internal waste rather than fragmenting the lists with stubs."," ","-- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in","-  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.","-  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.","-- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start","-  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and","-  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to","-  scan.","+Both doors fall through to the same fragmentation-recovery and growth","+machinery below when their free-lists can't satisfy a request."," ","-The linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for","-splits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows","-list traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary","-index — the API doesn't change.","+### Reference counting drives deallocation"," ","-### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)","+Every value the allocator hands out is reference-counted. The dispatch","+layer increments the count when handing a value to a consumer and","+decrements it when the consumer is done. When the count reaches zero,","+the chunk is returned to the allocator."," ","-For values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM","-responses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound","-is not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value","-directly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:","+The return-to-allocator step does two things atomically: pushes the","+chunk onto the appropriate free-list AND checks the chunk's two","+physical neighbors. If either neighbor is also free, the deallocator","+merges them into a larger chunk and pushes the merged chunk onto the","+free-list for the merged size. This eager neighbor-merge is O(1) and","+keeps small-scale fragmentation from accumulating on the hot path."," ","-```","-{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }","-```","+Reference counting requires touching every place that hands out a","+pointer to an allocator-managed value. That cost is paid once. After","+the wiring exists, both doors above benefit from the same recycling."," ","-`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a","-plain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.","-When a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:","-1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.","-2. Writes the bytes there.","-3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.","+### When does the bigger sweep run"," ","-The consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,","-copies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's","-refcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the","-large-value-heap region.","+The eager neighbor-merge above catches the common case. It misses","+patterns where free chunks are scattered with allocated chunks between","+them — the cheap merge can't see past its immediate neighbors."," ","-The slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.","-The two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still","-supporting unbounded outputs.","+A deeper sweep that walks the whole address-ordered chunk list","+looking for runs of contiguous free chunks runs on two deterministic","+triggers, both decoupled from wall-clock time:"," ","-A box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as","-\"variable-size\" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the","-fixed-size path with no indirection.","+1. **At the moment an allocation would otherwise fail.** When a","+   request can't be satisfied from any free-list — including after","+   trying larger classes and slicing — the system runs the deep sweep","+   before falling back to asking the operating system for more memory.","+   If the sweep produces a chunk large enough to satisfy the request,","+   the allocation succeeds and no growth happens. This is the","+   mandatory trigger: the sweep is the immediate alternative to","+   monotonic growth, and it fires exactly when its work has value."," ","-### Growth","-When all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy","-a request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,","-dividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class","-lists. Between batches is a natural opportunity","+   because no tasks are reading or writing chunks at that instant.","+   This is the opportunistic trigger."," ","-### Why this design","-- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single","-  pop from a list.
